expectations.text: Uses a discriminated union keyed on the status field
expectations.evidence: export type Subscription = | { status: "trialing"; ... } | { status: "active"; ... } | { status: "past_due"; ... } | { status: "canceled"; ... }

expectations.text: Each variant carries only its own fields, so e.g. a canceled subscription cannot hold a trial end date
expectations.evidence: Each variant lists only its own state fields: trialing has trialEndDate, canceled has cancelReason/voluntary; "Each variant carries *only* the fields that make sense for it"

expectations.text: Includes a compiler-enforced exhaustiveness check (assertNever or an equivalent never arm)
expectations.evidence: function assertNever(x: never): never { ... } ... default: return assertNever(sub);

expectations.text: Introduces distinct or branded types rather than bare strings for IDs
expectations.evidence: type Brand<T, B> = T & { readonly [brand]: B }; export type SubscriptionId = Brand<string, "SubscriptionId">;

expectations.text: Provides a single transition function or otherwise constrains how state changes
expectations.evidence: No transition function or allowed-transition type is given; only a read-only getStatusMessage handler. Nothing constrains moving between states.

expectations.text: Explicitly names which misuses the design makes impossible
expectations.evidence: "Misuse enumeration" list plus "sub.trialEndDate is a compile error until you've narrowed to status === "trialing"" and "Branded IDs mean transfer(subscriptionId, userId) is a type error"

expectations.text: Avoids a bag-of-optional-fields interface as the primary recommendation
expectations.evidence: Primary recommendation is the discriminated union; optional-field approach is called out as a hazard: "With optional fields, callers can construct nonsense."
